title: Emerging Legal Frameworks
answer: Machine authorship, autonomous entities, multi-agent liability, deepfake evidence and the right to an explanation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship is the line at which a work produced with generative systems becomes capable of attracting copyright or a comparable right.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries covers systems that act on someone's behalf with limited or no human sign off at the moment of action, from trading and procurement agents to software that manages money, data or care for a named beneficiary.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: Liability when agents interact covers the question of who answers for harm that arises when two or more autonomous AI agents transact, negotiate or coordinate with each other and something goes wrong.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes and evidentiary standards covers how courts, tribunals and regulators decide whether a piece of audio, video or image is what it claims to be, and what happens when it may be synthetic.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation is the idea that a person affected by an automated decision should be able to learn why that decision was made.

sections.body: This section covers the legal questions that appear once AI systems stop being tools and start producing things, making decisions, or acting alongside other systems. Machine authorship asks who owns or is credited with output a model generated, and whether that output can be protected at all. Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries examine arrangements where software holds or manages something on someone else's behalf, and what duties follow. Liability when agents interact looks at chains of action where several automated systems pass work to each other and something goes wrong. Deepfakes and evidentiary standards deal with proving what a recording or document actually is once synthesis is cheap. The right to an explanation concerns what a person is owed when an automated decision goes against them.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Almost nothing here is settled. Courts and legislatures have moved on some pieces, such as disclosure duties for synthetic media in a few jurisdictions and data protection rules that touch automated decisions, but the underlying concepts remain contested. Authorship rules were built for human creators and strain when a model generates text or images from a prompt, and no consistent answer exists on whether the prompter, the trainer, or nobody holds rights. Liability across interacting agents is harder still, because fault has to be traced through systems that may not log their reasoning. The honest limits are that most of this is argued from analogy to older law, that outcomes vary by jurisdiction, and that any summary here describes the debate rather than predicting how a specific dispute would end.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run from the most concrete question to the most procedural. The Threshold of Machine Authorship is the entry point, setting out why existing copyright and patent ideas struggle with generated work. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries moves from ownership to responsibility, covering what it means for software to hold a role rather than a product. Liability When Agents Interact takes that responsibility and spreads it across multiple systems, which is where causation gets difficult. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards turns to proof, since authentication problems now sit underneath every other question in this section. The Right to an Explanation closes the set by asking what a person can demand to know about a decision, which ties the earlier threads together. A reader new to the area should start with authorship, while someone facing a specific problem will likely go straight to the page matching it.
